summary: Describes a mechanism for layer-2 separation of stations that reach an IPv4 gateway over a bridged Ethernet segment. It uses an ARP proxy function so that stations cannot talk directly to each other and all traffic goes through the gateway. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: On a shared Ethernet line, one customer could reach another customer's computer directly, without the operator's router ever seeing the traffic. RFC 4562 describes a way to stop that: the equipment at the end of each line answers the customer's address requests with the router's address instead, and drops anything sent to another address.

questions: how does mac-forced forwarding isolate customers
subtitle: Keeping customers on a shared Ethernet access line from reaching each other directly, by answering their address lookups with the gateway.

tldr.problem: On an Ethernet access network several customers share one broadcast medium, so their hosts can see each other at layer 2 and attack each other directly, and the operator loses the place to police, filter and bill their traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The access node answers every ARP request from a subscriber line with the MAC address of an allowed access router, and discards any upstream unicast frame not addressed to one of those routers, so all traffic between customers has to pass through the router.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document describing a mechanism rather than a protocol. The mechanism is for IPv4 only, because IPv6 gives each customer its own prefix and resolves addresses with a different protocol.

today: RFC 4562 is an Informational document from June 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a mechanism rather than a protocol standard, and it says explicitly that it does not apply to IPv6 access networks, where each customer premises network is expected to be allocated its own prefix.

sections.title: Why an Access Network Needs Layer-2 Separation
sections.content:
The main purpose of an access network is to provide connectivity between customer hosts and service provider access routers, offering reachability to the Internet and other IP networks and to IP-based applications. An access network can be split into a subscriber line part and an aggregation network part. The subscriber line, often called the first mile, is an individual physical or logical connection to each customer premises. The aggregation network, the second mile, performs aggregation and concentration of customer traffic. The two are interconnected by an Access Node, which is the border between the individual subscriber lines and the common aggregation network.

The aggregation network connects to access routers, and in the figure of the document the access routers sit at the far edge of the aggregation network while the access nodes sit on the subscriber line side. An Ethernet access node is the specific kind of access node that supports Ethernet subscriber lines and uplinks to an Ethernet aggregation network.

Using Ethernet as the access technology has one consequence that shapes the whole design: traffic for different customers travels over a shared broadcast network. If the access nodes were ordinary Ethernet bridges, there would be direct layer 2 visibility between stations at different customer premises, and in particular between hosts in the same IP subnet. That breaks the separation requirement and creates a security problem, because a malicious customer can attack another customer's hosts directly at the Ethernet layer.
sections.plainLanguage: An access network joins each customer's line to a shared aggregation network. On Ethernet, all the customers share the same broadcast medium, so without extra work a customer's computer can reach a neighbour's computer directly and the operator never sees the traffic.

sections.title: Two Requirements and the Alternatives
sections.content:
Two basic requirements must be satisfied. The first is layer-2 separation between customer premises: all traffic to and from customer hosts at different premises must be forwarded via an access router, and not bridged or switched at layer 2, which enables the service provider to use the routers for security filtering, policing and accounting. The second is high IPv4 address assignment efficiency, because IPv4 address space is scarce. Efficiency improves if host addresses come from one or more large pools rather than from separate small subnet blocks allocated to each customer. IPv6 address assignment efficiency is of much less concern, and IPv6 deployments are expected to allocate separate subnet blocks to each customer premises.

In ATM-based access networks the separation is intrinsic, through ATM permanent virtual connections between the customer's access device and the access router, typically co-located with access control functionality in a Broadband Remote Access Server. Techniques other than ATM PVCs are needed for Ethernet access networks.

One option would be to implement access router functionality in each access node and treat each subscriber line as a separate IP interface, but that would mean routing inside the access network, which is often undesirable because of regulatory requirements for direct layer-2 accessibility to multiple IP service providers, and it would not solve the address efficiency requirement.

Two standardised solutions avoid routing. PPP over Ethernet creates individual PPP sessions between hosts and one or more Broadband Remote Access Servers over a bridged Ethernet topology, so traffic always flows between the server and hosts and never directly between hosts; the access node can force upstream traffic to flow only to the server the host selected. A VLAN per customer premises network separates each customer's traffic into different VLANs across the aggregation network between the access node and the access router.

Both provide layer-2 isolation, but neither is considered optimal for broadband access. PPPoE does not support efficient multicast, because packets must be replicated on each PPPoE session to the hosts listening on a group, which negates one of the main advantages of Ethernet and is especially problematic for services such as IPTV, where a channel may have hundreds or thousands of listening hosts. VLANs force multicast packets to be replicated to each VLAN with a listening host, and the limit of 4096 VLANs per Ethernet network restricts scalability, a limit that VLAN stacking can remove at the cost of more provisioning complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator wants two things: customers must not talk directly to each other, and the operator must not waste IPv4 addresses by giving every customer its own subnet. The two standard ways of isolating customers, PPP over Ethernet and one VLAN per customer, both make multicast expensive, which the mechanism in this document avoids.

sections.title: The ARP Proxy in the Access Node
sections.content:
The basic property of the solution is that the access node ensures upstream traffic is always sent to a designated access router, even when the IP traffic should ultimately flow between customer hosts in the same IP subnet. The solution has three parts: the access node obtains the IP and MAC addresses of the allowed target routers for each customer host, it replies to any upstream ARP request from a customer host with the MAC address of an allowed target router, and it discards any upstream unicast traffic to MAC addresses other than the allowed routers.

An access network may contain several routers, and different hosts may be assigned to different ones, so the access node must register the assigned router addresses per customer host. One of the routers acts as the default gateway for each host; if a customer has simultaneous access to several routers, the others typically give access to other IP networks. The access node learns the IPv4 addresses of the allowed routers in one of two ways, depending on how the host addresses are assigned. For each host using DHCP, the access node learns them dynamically by snooping the DHCPACK reply sent to the host. If a host needs simultaneous access to several routers, DHCP option 121 or option 33 must be used to name them. With static addressing, the router addresses must be provisioned in the access node by the network operator. In both cases the access node then uses ARP to determine the routers' MAC addresses, either immediately after learning the IP addresses or when they are first needed. The DHCP server can also associate hosts with subscriber lines if the access node uses the DHCP Relay Agent Information Option, option 82, to pass a subscriber line identifier upstream.

Now consider what happens when a host wants to reach another host at a different premises in the same IP subnet. It sends an ARP request to get that host's MAC address. The request is intercepted by the access node's ARP proxy, and an ARP reply is sent naming an allowed router MAC address, typically the default gateway's, in a manner similar to proxy ARP. The requesting host therefore registers a router MAC address as the layer 2 destination for any host in that IP subnet. A request for the IPv4 address of an allowed target router is answered with that router's own MAC address, not the default gateway's.

One exception is made. If a host asks for another host on the same premises network, the request should be discarded, because the target host is assumed to answer it directly. To recognise that case the access node must keep track of all the IPv4 addresses assigned on a subscriber line.
sections.plainLanguage: When a customer's computer asks the network which hardware address belongs to another customer's computer, the equipment at the end of the line answers with the address of the operator's router instead. The computer then sends its traffic to the router, and never learns the other customer's hardware address at all.

sections.title: Filtering Upstream Traffic
sections.content:
Because the ARP proxy always answers with a router MAC address, a well-behaved host never learns the MAC addresses of hosts at other premises. Malicious customers or malfunctioning hosts may still try to send traffic using other unicast destination MAC addresses, so the access node must discard all unicast frames received on a subscriber line that are not addressed to an allowed router. A customer host may also be allowed direct layer-2 access to one or more application servers attached directly to the aggregation network, and there is no functional difference in the way the mechanism treats access to routers and application servers.

Broadcast or multicast packets received on a subscriber line must never be forwarded on other subscriber lines, only on the uplinks to the aggregation network. The access node must discard all non-ARP broadcast packets received on subscriber lines, except that when DHCP is in use it must forward the client-to-server DHCP broadcast messages DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPREQUEST, DHCPDECLINE and DHCPINFORM upstream. It should rate limit upstream broadcast packets. Broadcast packets forwarded on an uplink may be forwarded to other access nodes by the aggregation network, so the access node should discard all broadcast packets received from the aggregation network, except ARPs from access routers for subscriber hosts and the server-to-client DHCP messages DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK and DHCPNAK.

Traffic between hosts in the same IPv4 subnet at different premises is always forwarded via a router, and the router forwards it back out of the interface it arrived on. That normally produces an ICMP redirect to the originating host, so the ICMP redirect function has to be disabled on the router's aggregation network interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The answering alone is not enough, because a customer can try to send directly anyway. So the equipment also drops any packet addressed to a hardware address other than the router's, and drops most broadcast traffic, letting through only the address lookups and the DHCP messages that are needed.

sections.title: Multicast, IPv6 and Resilience
sections.content:
Multicast traffic delivered from the aggregation network or further upstream is supported in a scalable way by Ethernet's native multicast capability. Bandwidth efficiency can be improved if the access node behaves as an IGMP snooping bridge, pruning the set of subscriber lines on which a group is forwarded. The access node must discard all IPv4 multicast packets received on a subscriber line other than IGMP Membership Report and Leave Group messages. A host that wants to source multicast packets to a group must tunnel them upstream to a multicast router, for example an access router acting as a PIM-SM Designated Router, and the router forwards them back into the access network if any customer hosts are listening.

MAC-Forced Forwarding is not directly applicable to IPv6 access networks. IPv6 access networks do not need the same address allocation efficiency, and it is expected that customer premises networks will be given unique network prefixes, such as a /48, that accommodate large numbers of customer subnets and hosts. IPv6 nodes also do not use ARP but the Neighbor Discovery Protocol for layer 2 address resolution. To support both IPv6 and MAC-Forced Forwarding for IPv4 at the same time, the access node can implement the unicast, broadcast and multicast filtering rules and learn the IPv6 and MAC addresses of the allowed routers either through static configuration or by snooping Router Discovery messages. Because multicast is intrinsic to the IPv6 protocol suite, the access node must not indiscriminately filter IPv6 multicast packets flowing upstream, although it may rate limit them.

The operation does not interfere with or delay IP connectivity recovery after a sustained router failure. Using DHCP to configure hosts with information about several redundant routers, or using VRRP for router redundancy, allows connectivity to be maintained. The mechanism is a stateful protocol: with static addressing the access node must be provisioned with state about the hosts reachable on a subscriber line and their routers, and after a transient failure that state can be recovered quickly from configuration storage. With DHCP it operates as a soft-state protocol, and because the DHCP and ARP messages that are snooped to build the state database are sent infrequently, a transient failure may not be detected by the routers or the hosts, so the access node should keep its dynamic state database in resilient storage. The access node is a single point of attachment between a subscriber line and the aggregation network, and therefore a single point of connectivity failure; customers wanting more resilience should multi-home.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism only covers IPv4, because IPv6 gives every customer its own address space and uses a different way of finding hardware addresses. The equipment also has to keep a record of which addresses belong to which customer, which means it should store that record somewhere that survives a reboot.

sections.title: What the Mechanism Guarantees
sections.content:
MAC-Forced Forwarding is, by its nature, a security function: it ensures layer 2 isolation of customer hosts sharing a broadcast access medium. In that sense it provides security equivalent to the alternative permanent virtual circuit based solutions. The security procedures appropriate for any shared access medium are equally appropriate when it is employed, and it does not introduce any additional vulnerabilities over those of standard Ethernet bridging.

In addition to layer 2 isolation, the access node must discard all upstream broadcast packets, except valid DHCP messages and ARP requests, which it proxies. In particular it must discard any DHCP server replies originating on a subscriber line, so a customer cannot pretend to be the DHCP server, and it may rate limit upstream broadcast DHCP messages.

Because the access node keeps track of the IPv4 addresses allocated on subscriber lines, it has enough information to discard upstream traffic with spoofed IPv4 source addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: As well as stopping customers reaching each other, the equipment can spot traffic that claims to come from an address the customer was never given, and can stop a customer from answering the DHCP requests meant for the real server.

items.title: Unicast to a non-router address
items.text: Discarded, unless the destination is an allowed access router or an allowed application server.

items.title: Broadcast on a subscriber line
items.text: Discarded, except ARP requests, which are proxied, and the client-to-server DHCP messages DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPREQUEST, DHCPDECLINE and DHCPINFORM.

items.title: Broadcast from the aggregation network
items.text: Discarded, except ARPs from access routers for subscriber hosts and the server-to-client DHCP messages DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK and DHCPNAK.

items.title: IPv4 multicast on a subscriber line
items.text: Discarded, except IGMP Membership Report and Leave Group messages. A host that wants to send multicast must tunnel it upstream to a multicast router.
